summary: Gives the architectural description and concept of operations for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP), an experimental, evolutionary enhancement to IP. It comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group and defines an Experimental Protocol.

eli5.summary: Today an IP address is both your name and your home address. ILNP splits them, so you keep your name when you move house. It is only an experiment.

questions: how does ilnp separate identity from location
why does splitting ip addresses enable mobility without special protocols
what are the benefits of ilnp multihoming over today's approach
how does ilnp work with existing ipv6 routers
subtitle: Separate identity from location to enable mobility and multihoming at the network layer.

tldr.problem: IP addresses conflate two separate concerns: they identify a node, and they also locate it topologically on the network. This entanglement makes mobility and multihoming difficult and breaks when nodes move or gain additional connections.
tldr.mechanism: ILNP splits the IP address into two distinct namespaces: an Identifier (non-topological, names the node) and a Locator (topological, names a network). Transport-layer protocols use Identifiers, which stay fixed for the duration of a session. Network-layer protocols use Locators, which can change as the node moves or adds connections, but change does not affect the transport-layer session.
tldr.outcome: Nodes can change network connectivity, achieve session survivability during mobility, and support both host and site multihoming with native protocol support rather than requiring special-case mechanisms like Mobile IPv6.

facts.label: Locator size (IPv4)
facts.value: Up to 30 bits (fits in address field)

facts.label: Router changes required
facts.value: None for IPv6; ARP enhancement only for IPv4

today: RFC 6740 documents ILNP as an Experimental Protocol published by the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF) Routing Research Group. ILNP has not been standardized for mainstream deployment and remains primarily of research interest. Various IRTF-affiliated research papers have explored ILNP, but it has not seen widespread implementation or production deployment in the Internet core or in common endpoint systems. It stands as a reference architecture for how identity-locator separation could be achieved.

sections.title: The Identity-Location Problem
sections.content:
The Internet has long recognized a fundamental problem: IP addresses carry overloaded semantics. An IPv4 address and an IPv6 address each serve two purposes simultaneously. They identify which node should receive the data, and they also indicate the topological location where that node is attached to the network. This dual role has roots in the original Internet architecture but creates friction for any scenario where a node's location changes independently from its identity.

Today, nodes work around this problem using special protocols. Mobile IPv6 lets a mobile node keep a home address while moving; the home agent acts as a proxy. Multihoming requires either managing multiple addresses (which breaks transparency) or deploying site-border routers and extra routing complexity. Both approaches add cost and operational burden.

ILNP proposes a direct architectural fix: split the overloaded IP address into two distinct, orthogonal namespaces with clear semantics, so that identity and location can evolve independently.
sections.eli5: Today, your home address says who you are and where you live. If you move, you need a forwarding agent or a new address. ILNP gives you a stable name and a separate changeable address, like a phone number and a mailing address.

sections.title: Identifiers and Locators
sections.content:
An Identifier (also called a Node Identifier or NID) is a non-topological name that uniquely identifies a node. It is bound to the node itself, not to any particular interface or attachment point. An Identifier uses the same 64-bit format as an IPv6 interface identifier (Modified EUI-64 syntax), but carries entirely different semantics: it names the node across all its interfaces and over time, regardless of where the node is connected. An Identifier is immutable once a transport-layer session begins; it forms part of the invariant end-to-end state, just like addresses do in IP today.

A Locator is a topologically significant name that identifies an IP subnetwork, analogous to a routing prefix. Locators have the same syntax as today's IP routing prefixes: 64 bits for IPv6, up to 32 bits for IPv4. A node may have multiple Locators (one per network attachment point), and Locators are dynamic—they change when the node moves, when it multihomes, or when upstream connectivity changes. Critically, Locators are used only for routing and forwarding; transport-layer protocols never see them.

Transport protocols (TCP, UDP, SCTP) use only the Identifier in their session state and checksum calculations. Routers use only the Locator for forwarding. This clean separation enables mobility (Locators change without affecting TCP state) and multihoming (a single Identifier binds to multiple Locators simultaneously) without special mechanisms.
sections.eli5: An Identifier is your name: stable, unique, yours for life. A Locator is where you are right now: your office, your home, your car. When you move offices, your name stays the same, only your Locator changes. When you have two phone lines, your name is still one, but you can be reached at two Locators.

sections.title: How ILNP Works in Practice
sections.content:
An ILNP node maintains an Identifier-Locator Communication Cache (ILCC) that stores its own valid Identifiers and Locators and learns about correspondent nodes' Identifiers and Locators from DNS. When a node initiates communication, it queries DNS for the peer's FQDN and receives not just address records (for backward compatibility) but also Node Identifier (NID) and Locator records (L64 for IPv6, L32 for IPv4). It stores these in the ILCC along with their Time-To-Live values.

When sending a packet, the node selects a source Identifier from its own ILCC (usually the only one it has), selects one of its valid Locators (based on local policy or preference), looks up the destination Identifier and Locator from the ILCC, and constructs the packet. For ILNPv6, the upper 64 bits carry the Locator and the lower 64 bits carry the Identifier, fitting exactly into the 128-bit IPv6 address space. Routers never see the distinction; they use the upper 64 bits (Locator) for longest-prefix matching, just like IPv6 prefixes today.

When a node's Locators change due to mobility or multihoming, it sends an ICMP Locator Update message to all active correspondent nodes, informing them of the new Locator set. Because the Identifier in transport-layer state does not change, the transport-layer session simply continues with the new Locator. The correspondent caches the new Locators and updates its own DNS records for future incoming sessions. No router changes are needed.
sections.eli5: You keep a list of your friends' names and addresses. When you call someone, you use your name and your current address, and ask for their name and address. When you move, you call and say, here is my new address but my name is the same. If you have two offices, people can reach you at either one, using the same name.

sections.title: Multihoming and Mobility Made Native
sections.content:
ILNP treats multihoming and mobility as two aspects of the same mechanism: managing Locator values over time. A multihomed host simply maintains multiple Locators in its ILCC and can choose any of them for each packet sent (or a transport-layer protocol can bind multiple Locators to one session, enabling multipath transport). When network connectivity fails on one path, the host can switch to another Locator without disrupting the transport-layer session, because the Identifier (which is what TCP cares about) does not change.

Mobile hosts behave similarly. As a node moves from one network to another, it receives IPv6 Router Advertisements or similar signals for the new Locator, stores it in the ILCC, and begins using it. Existing correspondent nodes learn of the change via the Locator Update message and update their cache. The transport-layer session continues transparently because the Identifier remains bound to the same TCP or UDP port tuple.

Critically, site multihoming in ILNP does not require provider-independent (PI) routing prefixes, which cause inter-domain routing scaling problems. A multihomed site can use provider-aggregated (PA) prefixes from multiple ISPs as Locators, bind them all to the same node Identifier, and achieve full session survivability. This solves the routing scalability problem that motivated much ILNP research.
sections.eli5: You can have a home office and a desk at a co-working space. Same name, two addresses. When someone calls, they use your name. If the line at one place is busy, calls go to the other. When you move to a new co-working space, you send an update, and only your address changes.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Router Transparency
sections.content:
ILNP is designed for incremental deployment with zero router changes. For ILNPv6, the Locator occupies the top 64 bits of the IPv6 address (exactly where a routing prefix goes today), so core routers treat ILNPv6 packets as ordinary IPv6 packets and forward them using normal longest-prefix matching. A router cannot tell whether a packet is IPv6 or ILNPv6; the packet format is identical.

ILNPv4 is more constrained (only 32 bits to work with), so Locators are at most 30 bits. Identifiers are carried in IPv4 options, which some routers and middleboxes may filter. Despite this complication, ILNPv4 still requires no changes to backbone routers.

Nodes that do not support ILNP continue to work normally with ILNP-capable nodes by using classic IP addresses. An ILNP-capable node can fall back to IP if it does not find ILNP records (NID and Locator records) in DNS. During the transition period, ILNP nodes advertise both classic IPv6/IPv4 address records and ILNP-specific records in DNS, so old and new systems interoperate seamlessly.
sections.eli5: ILNP works on today's routers. Old computers that do not know about it still work fine, because their regular address records are still in the DNS. New computers use the new records if they find them, and fall back to regular addresses if they do not.

layers.detail: IP: uses addresses for routing; ILNP: uses Locators (dynamic per connectivity)
